title: The fourth and fifth ways
hook: degrees of goodness and order in nature; thinkers still argue about these

segments.voice: Yesterday, the second and third ways: nothing makes itself, and things that can fail to be point to something that exists of itself. Your line was why anything at all. Where did that question catch you? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-eight.

An arrow leaves the bow and crosses the whole field into the center of the target. The arrow knows nothing. It doesn't aim. It doesn't want the bullseye. And yet, from a good archer's hand, it gets there. That arrow is Thomas Aquinas's own picture, the last image in his five ways. Two of the five are left, and thinkers, believers and not, still argue about them. So today has two jobs. Walk the last two ways. Then ask what an argument like this is actually for. Today's word: the fourth and fifth ways.
screen: `AN ARROW THAT DOESN'T AIM.` → `TWO WAYS LEFT.` → `WHAT IS AN ARGUMENT FOR?`

segments.voice: The fourth way starts from more and less. We call one act kinder than another, one answer truer, one life nobler. Thomas says more and less only make sense measured against a most. So there is something truest, best, noblest, and so most fully being, which causes the being and goodness in everything else. And this, he says, we call God. His example shows his age: fire, he says, is the hottest thing, the cause of heat in all the rest. That's the science he learned. The point he's after is goodness, not fire. The fifth way is the arrow. Things without minds, Thomas notices, still act for an end. An acorn heads for oak. Rain falls, plants turn toward light, and they do it regularly, not by luck. But a thing with no mind can't head for a goal unless someone with a mind directs it, as the archer directs the arrow. So there is someone intelligent who directs natural things to their ends. And this, he says, we call God. Notice what the fifth way is not. It isn't about how intricate a thing is. It's about how reliably mindless things lean toward a goal. The Psalm sings the same direction, in the Douay-Rheims: "The heavens shew forth the glory of God." Now the arguing. Thomas meant the five ways as real arguments. Readers, believing and not, still push on them: on the step from more to most, on whether nature's regularity needs a director. And here's something worth seeing. Thomas called them ways. A way doesn't drag you anywhere. You have to walk it, and weigh each step, and decide. He wrote them for beginners, in a book that states the other side first. An argument, for him, is an invitation to think, not a fist.
screen: `MORE AND LESS NEED A MOST.` · `MINDLESS THINGS ACT FOR AN END.` · `NOT INTRICACY, BUT DIRECTION.` · `A WAY HAS TO BE WALKED.` · then, large: `THE HEAVENS SHEW FORTH THE GLORY OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think about an argument you disagree with. Settle, and breathe. Choose one, about God or anything else that matters. This time, don't just restate it. Walk it. Take its first step: does that hold for you? Then the next, and the next, slowly, until you reach the exact step where you get off. Don't argue back. Just find the spot. Notice that the argument can't make you do anything. It can only invite. If you pray, you can ask for an honest mind. If you don't, just stay with the spot where you stepped off, and look at it. The bell holds the time.
The fourth and fifth ways. Thomas's arguments from degrees of goodness, which point to a most, and from order in nature, which points to a mind that directs. Today's word.
screen: `THE FOURTH AND FIFTH WAYS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: arguments invite, not force. Today, in one disagreement, offer your reasons and then stop pushing. Let the other person walk it. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: In Catholic classrooms the five ways are often taught as a set, with time given to the objections raised against them and to Thomas's own replies.

match.prompt: the fourth and fifth ways — tap the pairs.
pairs: more and less need a most
mindless things act for an end
directs the arrow to its mark

myth: the fifth way is about how intricate living things are
it's about things without minds reliably acting for an end, like an arrow sent to its mark.
Thomas's example in the fourth way is fire as the hottest thing
an example from the science he learned; the point he's after is goodness and being.
Thomas meant the five ways as idle guesses
he meant them as real arguments, and he called them ways: paths a person has to walk and weigh.

fork.setup: a friend tells you the fifth way doesn't convince them. what fits Thomas's own way of working?
options: tell them they just aren't thinking clearly.
state their objection fairly, then give your reply.
drop the subject and never raise it again.
fork.reveal: the Summa puts the objections first and answers each one. even in the article on the five ways, Thomas states the case against God's existence before he replies.

original.note: Latin: in five ways — Thomas writes that God's existence can be shown in five ways.

trapdoor: what you thought: knock-down proofs that end the conversation.
what it means: two more paths, from degrees of goodness and from order in nature, offered as reasons a person still has to weigh.
what a scholar hears: the fourth way leans on a most that causes the rest, with an old-physics example (fire); the fifth on things acting for an end, not on intricate design.

notes: ST I.2.3 fourth way paraphrased: more and less said by resemblance to a maximum; something truest, best, noblest, and so uttermost being; the maximum in a genus causes all in that genus (fire and heat, which Thomas takes from Aristotle); 'this we call God'. Fifth way: things lacking intelligence act for an end, always or nearly always the same way; directed by one with knowledge, as the arrow by the archer; 'this being we call God'. Confirm.
The acorn, rain and plants are the script's examples; Thomas speaks of natural bodies generally.
'Not intricacy, but direction' distinguishes the fifth way from later design arguments without naming them; confirm the framing.

'Readers, believing and not, still push on them' and 'thinkers, believers and not, still argue about them' are general statements from the outline hook ('thinkers still argue about these'); no counts given.
Douay-Rheims Psalm 18:2: confirm exact wording and verse numbering.
Original: ST I.2.3 reads 'Deum esse quinque viis probari potest'. Confirm.
